sections.heading: Living under your care and rule
sections.text: Jehovah God, you made everything, you hold everything together, and everything belongs to you. I cannot get away from your presence or step outside your rule—and I do not want to. It is a gift to live under your strong, righteous, wise, patient, merciful, and gracious hand.
theological_themes: God is Creator, Sustainer, and rightful owner of all things.
God's presence and sovereign rule are not a threat to the believer but a privilege and safety.
God's power is joined to righteousness, wisdom, patience, mercy, and grace.

scripture_references.connection: David recognizes that there is nowhere he can flee from God's presence, yet God's hand is still a guiding and holding hand. This supports the prayer's confidence that God's inescapable rule is a mercy, not merely a constraint.
Paul teaches that all things were created through Christ and are held together in him. This grounds the prayer's confession that God is the maker, sustainer, and owner of all things.

sections.heading: Seeing your heart clearly
sections.text: You love with a love deeper and better than even the best human parent. I admire your heart, trust your wisdom, tremble before your power, and humble myself before your holiness. Only when I see your goodness can my fear begin to quiet down. Your kindness is what draws me near instead of driving me away, and it is what helps me grieve over my sin and confess it honestly.
theological_themes: God's goodness draws sinners to repentance rather than excusing sin.
God is both holy and loving, both awesome in power and tender in mercy.
True confession grows from seeing God as he truly is.

scripture_references.connection: Paul says God's kindness is meant to lead people to repentance. This directly supports the prayer's claim that discovering God's goodness makes honest confession possible.
Because of Christ our great high priest, believers may draw near to God's throne for mercy and grace. This passage holds together reverence before God and confidence to approach him in need.

sections.heading: Coming to you with my real guilt
sections.text: When I look back at my guilt, and when I see how unworthy I still am, I feel afraid to come to you. I am dust. I have treated your goodness as if it were nothing, pushed against your power, and walked over your love. By my sin I have deserved death and judgment. I will not pretend otherwise.
theological_themes: Human beings are frail creatures before God.
Sin is personal rebellion against God's goodness, power, and love.
Apart from mercy, guilt before a holy God deserves judgment.

scripture_references.connection: After the fall, God reminds Adam that he is dust and will return to dust. This gives biblical weight to the prayer's humility about human frailty and mortality.

Paul identifies death as the wages of sin while also announcing eternal life as God's gift in Christ. This supports the prayer's sober confession that sin deserves death without making that the final word.

sections.heading: Needing the Savior you have given
sections.text: I cannot recover myself. Left to myself, I can ruin myself, but I cannot save myself. My help has to come from outside me. Thank you that you have placed salvation on the One who is strong enough to carry it—Jesus Christ. There is mercy with you, and in him there are riches of kindness I could never earn. Keep me always aware of how deeply I need him.
theological_themes: Salvation does not arise from human ability or moral improvement.
God provides a mighty Savior in Christ.
Mercy and grace come through Jesus, not through personal worthiness.

scripture_references.connection: This verse speaks of God laying help on one who is mighty. The original prayer draws on this language, and Christian prayer can receive it in light of God's saving provision through Christ.
Paul describes salvation as the result of God's mercy, love, and grace, not human works. This grounds the prayer's confession that rescue must come from God and is given in Christ.
Hebrews presents Jesus as able to save completely those who draw near to God through him. This supports the prayer's dependence on Christ as the sufficient Savior.

sections.heading: Let your joy keep me faithful to the end
sections.text: Restore to me the joy that comes from your salvation, and let that joy be my strength. Let it guard me when the world tries to pull my heart away from you. Let it hold up my mind and heart when comforts are taken from me. Let it give me life and courage when I walk toward death. Make me more and more like Christ, the Man from heaven. And even now, let me taste the first beginnings of the life that your angels and your people who are already with you know in fullness.
theological_themes: The joy of salvation strengthens obedience and endurance.
God's grace keeps believers from worldliness and sustains them through loss and death.
The Spirit forms believers into the likeness of Christ and gives them a foretaste of eternal life.

scripture_references.connection: David asks God to restore the joy of salvation and uphold him. This directly supports the prayer's request that restored joy would become sustaining strength.
Paul teaches that believers are being transformed into the image of the Lord. This grounds the prayer's desire to be shaped into the likeness of the heavenly Christ.
Paul contrasts the earthly man with the heavenly man and says believers will bear the image of the heavenly. This supports the prayer's hope that God will work the image of Christ in the believer.

Paul describes believers as having the firstfruits of the Spirit while they wait for full redemption. This fits the prayer's request for present foretastes of the life that will be fully known in God's presence.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original's statement that the speaker has made himself 'worthy of eternal death' is a strong Reformed/Puritan expression of guilt before God and final judgment. I preserved the force as 'deserved death and judgment' without softening it into merely emotional regret.

The phrase about enjoying the spirituality known by 'angels and departed saints' assumes conscious blessedness with God after death. I rendered it as tasting now the beginnings of the life known fully by angels and God's people already with him, avoiding speculation beyond the prayer's intent.
significant_interpretive_choices: I treated 'Creator, Upholder, Proprietor of all things' as a confession that God made, sustains, and owns everything, rather than as three abstract titles.

I rendered 'under the agency of omnipotence, righteousness, wisdom, patience, mercy, grace' as living under God's active hand, because the point is not bare power but God's personal rule exercised through his holy and gracious character.
I understood 'thou hast laid help on One that is mighty' as pointing to God's appointed Savior, fulfilled for Christian prayer in Jesus Christ, while retaining the biblical echo of Psalm 89:19.
I rendered 'the image of the heavenly' as becoming more like Christ, the Man from heaven, because the phrase echoes Paul's contrast between Adam and Christ in 1 Corinthians 15.
